paras: The Marion election riot and Vance house siege was a pair of linked shootings on November 8, 1881, election day, at Marion Station in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, about five miles from Meridian. After four white men were killed or mortally wounded at the polls, a sheriff's posse of about 100 men besieged the house of Ed Vance, a white Republican, and killed his son John, while a posse member, A. G. Warren, was shot dead from the house. Wire reports blamed armed Black men and the Vances, but Republican correspondents later published a version in which white Democrats began the shooting.

A Republican correspondent described Marion as the only Republican precinct in a 'hopelessly Democratic' county, with 'trouble' at every election. Ed Vance was described as a white man and the acknowledged leader of the county's Republicans.

According to the first Associated Press dispatch, Black men opened fire on unarmed whites at the polls, killing four, among them A. T. Harvey, the Democratic candidate for county assessor. A November 10 recapitulation said Joseph Barnett was shot after raising his arm at a Black man who had insulted him, named five Black men as the shooters, and said Will Vance was said to have urged them on.

Sheriff R. L. Henderson's first party was refused a surrender at Vance's house, two miles from the polls, and driven off by fire; reinforced, the sheriff surrounded the house at about five in the afternoon. In the wire version John Vance, aged 21 or 22, rode up and pointed a gun at the posse and was shot dead, and Warren was killed from inside the house. E. H. Dial, writing to the Democratic state committee that night, said Mrs. Vance had come out with a white flag and the sheriff had promised protection before Warren was shot at the well. Ed Vance escaped by the back, Will Vance was captured and jailed, and Black men fleeing the house were fired on; the November 10 dispatch said four or five were wounded and none known killed.
Martin Malone and four more Black men were jailed in the following days. An anonymous letter at Meridian ordered Black mail route agents to resign over the 'trouble caused by your race' at Marion.

In December Will Vance underwent a preliminary examination at Meridian as an accessory to the murders at the polls. Posse witnesses testified that the house fired first and that John Vance was trying to shoot toward C. P. Dement when killed, and a doctor's testimony showed that Bob Brown, a Black man, had died a week after the riot of wounds from the posse received 'while resisting arrest.' The state closed on December 28; no outcome and no inquest appear in the coverage.

The AP dispatches ran the next day in papers from Maine to California. The Savannah Morning News headed them 'Murder at the Polls' and 'A Fusilade from Negro Ruffans,' and the Jackson Comet printed Dial's letter as 'The Massacre at Marion.' In December the Memphis Appeal called Will Vance the 'Principal Instigator and Prime Mover' of the killings.

Republican papers doubted the wire story. One Daily Republican advised reading the November 10 dispatch 'with several grains of allowance' and later headed a New York Times correspondent's account 'A Shot Gun Story Spoiled.' The National Republican called the examination 'The Farce of a Mississippi Trial,' and the Corvallis Gazette said 'the Mississippi plan' was still in operation.

The New York Times correspondent wrote that a drunken Barnett struck a Black man, that whites fired first, and that the house held only the four Vances, a white Democrat and an old Black man, who was killed along with John Vance. The National Republican's correspondent said John had taken no part in the fight and was shot riding up while Warren threatened Mrs. Vance, that a brother then shot Warren, and that several fleeing Black men were killed. One news summary called John Vance 'colored.'

reader.title: Marion election riot and Vance house siege
bases: After the shooting at the Marion polls, a sheriff's posse of 75 to 100 men besieged Ed Vance's house to make arrests and killed John Vance and shot at Black men fleeing the house (A3, A13, A15, A18); Bob Brown, a Black man, later died of wounds from the posse (A34, A35).

A sheriff-led posse carrying arrest warrants killed John Vance and wounded fleeing Black men during an exchange of fire at the Vance house (A3, A15, A37); Republican accounts called the posse a 'mob' that pressed on against the sheriff's wishes (A25, A27), but no report describes a killing outside an attempted arrest.

Independent AP, Mississippi, Democratic-letter and Republican-correspondent accounts agree that the posse besieged the Vance house and that John Vance and A. G. Warren were killed (A3, A13, A18, A25, A27), though they disagree sharply on how.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatches from Meridian
accounts.gist: Armed Black men killed four unarmed whites at the polls and barricaded themselves with Ed Vance; John Vance pointed a gun at the posse and was shot, and Warren was killed from the house.

accounts.label: AP recapitulation, Nov. 10
accounts.gist: Barnett was shot after raising his arm at a Black man who insulted him; Will Vance was said to have set the shooting off; John Vance was shot crouching behind a stable with a gun levelled; no Black men known killed.

accounts.label: Democratic letter (E. H. Dial)
accounts.gist: Mrs. Vance came out with a white flag and the sheriff promised protection, then Warren was shot at the well; Ed Vance slipped out the back and fleeing Black men were shot in the bushes.

accounts.label: New York Times correspondent
accounts.gist: A drunken Barnett struck a Black man and whites fired first on fleeing Black men; the house held only the Vances, a white Democrat and an old Black man; the crowd fired on them as they tried to leave and John Vance was 'shot to pieces'.

accounts.label: National Republican Meridian letter
accounts.gist: Barnett and the Segars brothers began the fight; John Vance, uninvolved, was shot riding up while Warren threatened Mrs. Vance, and a brother then shot Warren; several Black men were killed fleeing.

accounts.label: State witnesses at the examination
accounts.gist: The house answered the surrender demand with an oath and a volley; the sheriff was shot at in the yard; John Vance was trying to shoot at a posse member when killed.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed the wire story 'Murder at the Polls' and 'A Fusilade from Negro Ruffans'; the Comet titled Dial's letter 'The Massacre at Marion'.
Most papers outside the South ran the AP dispatches without comment under heads such as 'A Mississippi Battle'.
The Memphis Appeal headed the December testimony with Will Vance as 'Principal Instigator and Prime Mover' of a massacre of 'Four Innocent Men'.
Republican papers called the wire story a 'Shot Gun Story', the examination 'The Farce of a Mississippi Trial', and the affair 'the Mississippi plan'.
